## Methods

Chemicals and materials
Iridium(IV) oxide (IrO2, ≥ 99.9%, 206237), NafionTM solution (5 wt.%, 274704), 3-(Trimethylsilyl)propionic-2,2,3,3-d4 acid sodium salt (TSP, ≥ 98.0% (NMR), 269913), Polytetrafluoroethylene preparation (PTFE solution, 60% in H2O, 665800), Deuterium oxide (D2O, 99.9 at.% D, 151882), Silver nitrate (AgNO3, ≥ 99.0%, 209139), Water-18O (H218O, ≥ 10 at.% 18O, 332089), α−terpineol (90%, 432628), 2-(2-butoxyethoxy)ethanol (≥ 99%, 579963), Oleylamine (70%, O7805), acetone (≥ 99.5%, 179124), Copper(I) chloride (CuCl, 97%, 212946), n-hexane (C6H14, 99%, HX0293), Octadecylamine (≥ 99%, 305391), Ethyl 2-cyanoacrylate (E1505, 7085-85-0), Trioctylphosphine (90%, 117854) and squalane (96%, 234311) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The alkaline ionomer solution (5% in ethanol, Sustainion XA-9) and anion exchange membrane (Sustainion X37-50) were purchased from Dioxide Materials. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥ 85.0%), stainless-steel mesh (SSM, 0.10 mm thickness, 500×500 mesh; warp, ~25 μm) and Titanium fiber felt (0.25 mm thickness, 99.9%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (China). Acrylic resin (E0545) was purchased from Shenzhen JITIAN Chemical Co., LTD. Isopropanol (C3H8O, IPA, ≥ 99.5%, 3776) was purchased from Fisher Scientific. The anion exchange membrane (Fumasep FAA-3-PK-75), gas diffusion layer (carbon paper, GDE, Sigracet 39BC), and Nafion® 117 membrane (591239) were purchased from Fuel Cell Store.

Catalyst synthesis
In a typical synthesis, 0.07 g of AgNO3 and 0.02 g of octadecylamine were dissolved in 0.8 mL of squalane, and the solution was heated for 0.5 h at 80 °C under an inert gas (Ar) atmosphere to form an Ag-based stock solution. Meanwhile, a mixed solution of 10 mL oleylamine and 0.04 mL trioctylphosphine was heated to 170 °C under an Ar atmosphere with vigorous magnetic agitation. Subsequently, the Ag-based stock solution was injected into the above mixture and heated to 170 °C for 5 h. After natural cooling, the resulting sample was collected by centrifugation and washed several times with n-hexane. Finally, the sample was dried at 80 °C in a vacuum before use. The sample was denoted as SS-Ag.

The SS-Ag samples were annealed at various temperatures (250, 350, and 450 °C) in the tube furnace for 2 h under a mixed gas (H2/Ar: 5 v/v%; 200 sccm), denoted as Ag-250, Ag-350, and Ag-450, respectively.

The Cu sample (SS-Cu) was also prepared by the above method, using a Cu-based stock solution (CuCl) instead of the Ag-based stock solution, and the reaction temperature was increased to 200 °C (see ref. 9 for more detailed information).

GDEs fabrication
For conventional/traditional CP-GDEs in the flow cell, carbon paper (Sigracet 39BC) served as the gas diffusion layer. The cathode catalyst was dispersed in a mixed solution of H2O and IPA (1:4 v/v) and a NafionTM solution (~3 wt.% vs. catalyst) by sonication for 1 h to form the catalyst ink (1 mg/mL). Then, the catalyst ink was sprayed onto the microporous carbon layer of the carbon paper at a catalyst loading of 1–3 mg/cm2, followed by drying at 120 °C under vacuum for 1 h before testing. The anode GDE using the commercial IrO2 as the anode catalyst was also prepared by the above method.

For conventional/traditional CP-GDEs used in the APMA MEA cell with pure H2O as the anolyte, the NafionTM solution in the cathode catalyst ink was replaced by an alkaline ionomer solution (Sustainion XA-9), and nothing else changed. In addition, Ir-supported Ti fiber felt (Ir/Ti) was used as the anode electrode. Ir was sputtered on the Ti fiber felt using a pure Ir target in an Ar environment (5×10-3 Torr) in a magnetron sputtering system. Then, Ir/Ti was pressed onto the carbon paper to form the anode GDE.

For high-diffusion-flux (HDF) GDEs, the cathode catalyst (SS-Ag/SS-Cu) was printed onto the SSM skeleton by screen printing, followed by vacuum drying overnight. After that, the SSM-skeleton-supported catalyst was pressed at 1000 pounds of pressure for 2 h and the thickness of the HDF-GDE was controlled to ~300 μm. Finally, it was calcined at 350 °C for 30 min. The printing ink was prepared by mixing the catalyst and PTFE solution with an organic solution consisting of α-terpineol, 2-(2-butoxyethoxy)ethanol, and acrylic resin, with an approximate weight ratio of 65:15:20. The catalyst loading in HDF-GDE was controlled to about 10 mg/cm2.

Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction measurements
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECO2R) in the flow cell was to employ an electrochemical workstation (CHI 660E) connected to a current booster (CHI 680C). The CO2 flow rate (30 sccm, unless otherwise noted) was controlled by a mass flow controller (MFC, Alicat Scientific MC). The electrolyte (1 M KOH, pH = ~14) flow rate was ~10 mL/min, controlled by a peristaltic pump. The cathode area in the flow cell was 1 cm×1 cm. The flow cell consists of two titanium gas flow channels, two PTFE buffer layers, a membrane (Fumasep FAA-3-PK-75) between the two buffer layers, two titanium current collectors, and two aluminum end plates. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel to guide the CO2 stream and conduct the electricity. The serpentine flow channel is featured with a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. Both cathode and anode chambers have two 0.5-cm-thick PTFE buffer layers, through which the 1 M KOH electrolyte stream flows. All ECO2R measurements in the flow cell were carried out at room temperature and the Hg/Hg2Cl2 (SCE, saturated KCl) was used as the reference electrode, and all cathode potentials (vs. Hg/Hg2Cl2) were converted to the RHE scale via the following Eq. 1:

E(RHE) = E(Hg/Hg2Cl2) + 0.241 + 0.0591 × pH + iR (1)

where R is the resistance between the cathode and reference electrodes in the flow cell measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) with a frequency range from 105 Hz to 0.01 Hz at the working potential.

For ECO2R in the single MEA cell, pure H2O (pH = ~7) was used as the anolyte. The cathode area in the flow cell was 1 cm×1 cm. The MEA cell consists of two titanium gas flow channels and a membrane between the cathode and the anode. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel, which has a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. The cathode and anode GDEs were separated by an AEM (Sustainion X37-50) and a PEM (Nafion 117) assembly (APMA architecture). The areas of both AEM and PEM are 2 cm×2 cm. AEM with a dry thickness of ~50 μm is soaked in 1 M KOH solution for storage and is washed with water before use. For the PEM with a dry thickness of ~183 μm, it was soaked in ~3% hydrogen peroxide for 1 h at 80 °C, deionized water for 1 h at 80 °C, and 0.5 M H2SO4 for another 1 h at 80 °C. And the resulting PEM was cleaned and preserved in deionized water at room temperature. Therein, the cathode GDE and the anode GDE were in contact with the AEM and the PEM, respectively. Cell voltages were directly presented without iR compensation for all MEA measurements. The reaction temperature was set at 60 °C. Unless otherwise noted, other reaction conditions were the same as those tested in the flow cell.

For scaled-up APMA-MEA stack measurements, an integrated circuit based on the Arduino UNO R3 (A000066) was used as an aid for monitoring, connected to the CoolTerm serial terminal application. The scaled-up APMA-MEA stack consists of two titanium gas flow channels and membranes between the cathode and the anode. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel, which has a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. All ECO2R measurements in the APMA-MEA stack were performed using the customized Variable DC power supply (10 kW). The cathode area was 150 cm2. The flow rates of the anolyte and CO2 were 20 mL/min and 3000 sccm, respectively. The initial temperature of the pure H2O anolyte was set to 30 °C rather than 60 °C due to the higher heat generation from the stack at high power. AEM (Sustainion X37-50) was replaced by one (MTCP-50) for the high stability30. Full-cell-stack voltages were directly presented without iR compensation. Unless otherwise noted, other reaction conditions were the same as those tested in the single MEA cell.

Products analysis
For ECO2R, the gas and liquid products were quantified by gas chromatography (GC, GC-2030, Shimadzu) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, ECZ500R, 500 MHz, JEOL), respectively. GC was equipped with two thermal conductivity detectors (TCDs) for H2, O2, N2, He, CO, and CO2 signals, and a flame ionization detector (FID) for CH4, C2H4, and C2H6 signals. GC was composed of packed columns of two Porapak-N, a Molecular sieve-13X, a Molecular sieve-5A, a Porapak-Q and an HP-PLOT AL/S, and employed He (99.999%) and N2 (99.999%) as the carrier gases. Ar was used as the internal standard to calibrate the CO2 flow rate at the cell outlet (fCO2), which was fed at 2 sccm and mixed with the cell outlet gas stream before injection into GC23. The FEs of gas products were calculated by the following Eq. 2:

FE(%) = N_x × F × m_x × f_CO2 / j_Total × 100% (2)

where N_x is the number of electrons transferred for the specific product (x), F is the Faradaic constant, m_x is the molar fraction of the specific product (x) determined by GC, f_CO2 is the molar flow rate of the CO2, and j_Total is the total current density.

The liquid products were analyzed by 500 MHz 1H NMR spectroscopy (ECZ500R, JEOL) with water suppression. TSP and D2O were used as the reference standard and lock solvent, respectively. The FEs of liquid products were calculated by the following Eq. 3:

FE(%) = N_x × F × C_x × V_x / Q_Total × 100% (3)

where N_x is the number of electrons transferred for the specific liquid product (x), F is the Faradaic constant, C_x is the concentration of the specific liquid product (x) determined by 1H NMR, V_x is the volume of the electrolyte, and Q_Total is the total charge.

CO2 conversion was calculated using the following Eqs. 4–6:

f_x = F_x / (N_total × t × x_A) (4)

For SS-Ag catalyst:

CO2 Conversion (%) = f_CO2 / f_CO2_inlet × 100% (5)

For SS-Cu catalyst:

CO2-to-C2H4 Conversion (%) = 2 × f_C2H4 / f_CO2_inlet × 100% (6)

where f_x is the molar rate of the product (x) formation, t is the electrolysis reaction time, and A is the geometric area of the electrode.

Multiphysics simulation
The simulation was performed using COMSOL Multiphysics v. 5.6. The ECO2R process at the cathode was simulated under a fixed inlet flow rate, steady-state conditions, and involves two half-reactions: ECO2R-to-CO and HER (Eqs. 7 and 8). Although HER can affect CO2 diffusion through convection between H2 and CO2, the resulting diffusion trends for CO2 and H2 are in agreement. Thus, to simplify the calculation, Eq. 8 was not considered during the simulation.

CO2 + H2O + 2e− → CO + 2OH− (7)

2H2O + 2e− → H2 + 2OH− (8)

The momentum conservation in the serpentine channel, porous gas diffusion electrode and catalyst layer is expressed by the compressible Navier-Stokes equation31 and Darcy’s law32, respectively (Eqs. 9–11):

ρ∇·u = 0 (9)

ρ(u·∇)u = ∇·[−pI + μ(∇u + (∇u)T)] (10)

μ/K u + ∇p = 0 (11)

where ρ, u, p and μ represent density, flow velocity, gauge pressure and dynamic viscosity, respectively. K represents the permeability of the porous structure, including the GDE and catalyst layer, which can be expressed as (Eq. 12):

K = d_f^2 × ε^3 / K_CK(1−ε)^2 (12)

where ε is the porosity, d_f is the mean fiber diameter or the size of the particle, and K_CK is the Carman-Kozeny constant. The specific surface area (a) (ref. 33) of the porous structure can be expressed as (Eq. 13):

a = 4(1−ε) / d_f (13)

The mass transfer of gas in the porous structure and the flow channel involves both convection and diffusion. Therefore, the mass transfer process of all participating particles can be expressed by the Maxwell-Stefan equation (Eqs. 14–18) (ref. 34):

∇·j_i + ρ(u·∇)ω_i = R_i (14)

j_i = −(ρω_i Σ D_ik ∇x_k + D_i^T ∇T / T) (15)

d_k = ∇x_k + [(x_k − ω_k) ∇p / p] (16)

x_k = ω_k / M_k / Σ (ω_i / M_i) (17)

ω_i = c_i M_i / ρ (18)

where the subscript i represents species type. j_i is the relative mass flux vector, ω_i is the mass fraction, D_ik is the Maxwell-Stefan diffusion coefficient, d_k is the diffusional driving force, D_i^T is the thermal diffusion coefficient, x_k is the molar fraction, M_i is the reciprocal of the molar mass, and p is the absolute pressure.

The transport of current in the electrocatalysis process occurs via electron transport at the electrodes. Therefore, they can be calculated through Ohm’s law (Eq. 19):

i_s = −σ_eff^s ∇φ_s (19)

where i_s and φ_s are the current density and potential, respectively. And the relationship between effective conductivity (σ_eff^s) and electrode material conductivity (σ_s) can be expressed by the Bruggeman correlation (Eq. 20) (ref. 35):

σ_eff^s = (1−ε)^1.5 σ_s (20)

The relationship of electrochemical reaction kinetics in the catalyst layer is described by the Butler-Volmer equation (Eq. 21) (ref. 36):

i_cs = i_0 [ (c_CO2 / c_CO2_ref) exp(α_c F η_c / RT) − (c_CO / c_CO_ref) exp(α_a F η_c / RT) ] (21)

where the i_cs stands for the transfer current density of the cathode. c_i and c_i_ref are the surface concentration and bulk concentration of the porous structure, respectively. α_c and η_c are the cathode charge transfer coefficient and the cathode overpotential, respectively. Here, i_0 represents the exchange current density of the cathode, which can be given as follows (Eq. 22) (ref. 36):

i_0 = F · k_c · (c_CO2)^α_c · (c_CO)^α_a (22)

where the k_c is the electrochemical reaction rate constant.

The overpotential can be expressed as follows (Eq. 23):

η_c = φ_s − φ_l − E_eq (23)

where subscripts s and l represent the solid phase and liquid phase, respectively. E_eq stands for the equilibrium potential. The Nernst equation can be used to describe the equilibrium potential as follows (Eq. 24):

E_eq = E^0 + RT / nF ln(c_CO2 / c_CO) (24)

where E^0 represents the standard electrode potential of the cathode versus the standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K.

Boundary conditions for the cathode half-reaction in the alkali-cation-free APMA system are as follows. The galvanostatic condition was used during the electrocatalytic process; hence, a constant current density was utilized on the current collector. In addition, a fixed mass flux (Q) and species mass fraction of CO2 were set at the inlet boundary and other boundary conditions were listed in Supplementary Table 1. The relevant transport parameters in the present simulation are listed in Supplementary Table 2. To ensure the numerical model accurately simulates the electrochemical reaction process, the electrochemical reaction validation was carried out under fixed operating conditions.

It can be seen that, across different CO2 inlet flow rates, the simulated CO/CO2 outlet flow rate is in good agreement with the experimental data (Supplementary Fig. 1). The slight deviation maybe attributed to the model’s omission of a side reaction. Therefore, the model could be used to simulate the electrochemical reaction process. To select the appropriate number of grids, the model calculates the corresponding pressure drop and CO2 concentration for different numbers of grids, and the results are listed in Supplementary Table 3. The data show that the differences in pressure drop and CO2 concentration across different grid numbers are small (about 0.11%). As the number of grids increases from 55751 to 75673, the pressure drops, and the CO2 concentration is grid-independent. Therefore, given the time and computational resource requirements, it can be concluded that the grid-dependent effect can be avoided when 55751 meshes are used to simulate the cathode ECO2R at the macroscopic scale.

Techno-economic analysis
The TEA of the CO2 electrolysis system is based on published models37,38, with slight adjustments to account for the recycling of unreacted CO2, thereby offsetting the cost of purchasing CO2. An industrial-scale production capacity of 50,000 kg/day is assumed. The actual single-pass conversion rate of CO2, derived from experimental studies, was utilized in the calculations. A pressure swing adsorption (PSA) unit was virtually designed to purify gaseous products from both the cathode and anode. The capital investment for the PSA unit was estimated based on reference costs, and its operating expenditure was calculated at 0.23 kWh per m3/h of gas mixture39. For typical electrodes, the membrane replacement cost was simplified to be 1180 $/m2 for all cases39. The parameters and assumptions used for TEA are summarized in Supplementary Table 4 and the TEA results are listed in Supplementary Tables 5 and 6.

The levelized cost of carbon monoxide production (LCOC) is employed as the techno-economic indicator, as defined in Eq. 25.

LCOC = Σ (TAC + OPEX_r)t / Σ (PD + D_r)t (25)

where TAC and WCP are the total annual cost and working capital, respectively. BAL is the balance of the plant. PD is the annual amount of product generated, which is 5000 kg/day for all case studies. r is the nominal interest rate and n is the plant lifetime.

Total annual cost is composed of the operating expenditure OPEX, and the depreciation cost DEP of the capital assets, as defined in Eq. 26.

TAC = OPEX + DEP (26)

where the calculation of OPEX includes the purchase cost of electricity and water, the replacement cost of membrane and stack, the purchase cost of carbon dioxide, maintenance cost, and operating expenses of the PSA unit. The depreciation rate of capital assets is assumed to average 10% annually until reaching 20% of the end-of-life salvage value of the facility37.

In-situ ECO2R Raman measurements
In-situ Raman measurements were carried out by a customized spectro-electrochemical flow cell fabricated with a sapphire window (thickness: 0.15 ± 0.02 mm; area: 1.4 cm×1.4 cm) in front of the cathode GDE. The Ni felt was used as a counter electrode. The overall system was operated in a two-electrode setup. The electrolyte was pumped through a sapphire window at a constant flow rate of 5 mL/min using a peristaltic pump over the cathode GDE, and the electrolyte layer thickness on the cathode surface was 1.5 mm. CO2 was supplied to the back of the cathode GDE through the serpentine flow channel to guide the CO2 at a flow rate of 30 sccm controlled by an MFC (Alicate Scientific MC). Raman spectra were collected under an accumulation time of 4 s and an accumulation number of 10 times using a WITEC Confocal Raman microscope with an objective (50×) and a 633 nm laser. The cell voltage was applied in potentiostatic mode and recorded without iR compensation.

In-situ heating TEM measurements. In-situ heating TEM measurements were performed on the JEOL Model JEM-2100F at 200 kV with a Fusion Select holder (Protochips) and a holey carbon-coated microelectromechanical system E-chip.

Materials characterizations
TEM images were collected on a JEOL JEM-2100F at 200 kV. SEM images were obtained on the field-emission Tescan MAIA3. ## Paper

## Abstract

Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECO2R) presents a sustainable pathway for industrial decarbonization by converting CO2 into carbon-neutral fuels and chemicals. Despite progress in catalyst design, industrial scalability is hindered by slow mass-transfer kinetics. Here, we introduce a high-diffusion-flux gas diffusion electrode (HDF-GDE) that overcomes this limitation in alkali-cation-free systems, achieving CO2 conversion rates at industrial current densities. Kinetic analysis demonstrates that conversion is governed by mass transfer efficiency rather than flow rate. By optimizing the GDE structure to maximize CO2 diffusion and GDE utilization, we realize a kW-scale ECO2R system with stability (>1000 hours), producing CO or C2H4 depending on the catalyst. Operating with a 3 L/min CO2 flow rate, the system delivers 144 kg of CO (1.29 kW) or 17 kg of C2H4 (1.95 kW) over 1000 h. The alkali-cation-free ECO2R system, equipped with HDF-GDEs, demonstrates economic viability for large-scale ECO2R-to-CO/C2H4 production. Our findings bridge the gap between lab innovation and real-world deployment, advancing carbon-neutral chemical manufacturing.

---

## Introduction

The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECO2R) technology, as a vital technical link between fossil fuel and sustainable energy, is considered one of the most promising options for rapidly cutting CO2 emissions at the industrial level 1–3. In order to improve its practical feasibility, the ECO2R technology has advanced from the H cell to flow and membrane-electrode-assembly (MEA) cells utilizing the gas diffusion electrode (GDE) (Fig. 1) (refs. 4,5). However, their stabilities were still problematic (e.g., carbonate formation and crossover) (refs. 6–8). More recently, MEA system stability has been improved by approximately one order of magnitude (>1000 h for ECO2R-to-C2H4) using an alkali-cation-free (pure-H2O-fed) MEA system9. Still, the low current density (only ~120 mA/cm2 towards C2H4) resulted in limited product yield (low CO2 conversion: ~1% for ECO2R-to-C2H4), fatally hindering the industrialization of the ECO2R technology.

The ECOR MEA cell with GDEs was derived from the fuel cell community (Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Fig. 2) (refs. 10–13). However, the ECOR system is more complicated than the fuel cell one (see Supplementary Note 1) (refs. 1,14). Taking the carbon paper GDE (CP-GDE) as an example, for ECOR, at the cathode, the H2 from the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), multiple products, and unreacted CO2 make the mass transfer in the system complicated (Fig. 1b). This results in irreconcilable contradictions between the high ECOR product selectivity (Faradaic efficiency: FE) and the high CO2 conversion (see Supplementary Note 1, and Supplementary Fig. 3 and Table 7 for more information). That is, lowering the reactant CO2 inlet flow rate could increase CO2 conversion, but this could considerably decelerate CO2 mass transfer kinetics in CP-GDE and decrease product selectivity.

To achieve both high CO2 conversion and high product selectivity, we proposed the high-diffusion-flux GDE (HDF-GDE) that consists only of the catalyst (Fig. 1d). HDF-GDE can allow CO2 to diffuse directly into the catalyst layer without having to pass through the inert CP-GDE substrate (Fig. 1e). This could not only significantly increase the overall flux of species both to and from the HDF-GDE but also greatly enhance the space utilization of GDE. From a chemical kinetics perspective, HDF-GDE could accelerate the system’s mass transfer kinetics, increasing CO2 and key reaction intermediate coverage (such as *CO) on the catalyst surface and decreasing the coverage of *H from water transfer15. This could improve ECO2R activity due to first-/second-order dependence on CO2/*CO coverage1,15.

In this study, we aimed to achieve a high operating current density (i.e., high CO2 conversion) in a high-stability alkali-cation-free ECO2R system while maintaining high product selectivity by accelerating mass transfer kinetics. Here, the alkali-cation-free condition contains trace amounts of sodium ions originating from the water source9. To achieve this, we developed an HDF-GDE comprising the catalyst and a stainless-steel mesh skeleton in the catalyst’s middle layer. A high-performance stepped-surface Ag (SS-Ag) catalyst was used as a model catalyst to study the system’s mass-transfer kinetics, given its single-product selectivity (i.e., CO). As a result, by improving the mass transfer efficiency, the current density of the alkali-cation-free ECO2R-to-CO system was increased from 150 to 400 mA/cm2 while maintaining high product FE (~93%). To further improve CO2 conversion and advance the industrialization of ECO2R technology, we designed and customized a kW-scale alkali-cation-free MEA cell stack assembled with HDF-GDEs to evaluate the entire system’s stability. At a power of ~1.29 kW (60 A) and 3 L/min CO2 inlet flow rate, CO2 conversion broke 81% with a CO FE of ~90%. Furthermore, the HDF-GDE strategy was also successfully applied to ECO2R-to-C2H4. At ~1.95 kW (75 A) and 3 L/min CO2 inlet flow rate, CO2 conversion for ECO2R-to-C2H4 was increased to ~15 times. Their system stability was over 1000 hours, yielding ~144 kg CO and ~17 kg C2H4, respectively. Real-time analysis of mass transfer kinetics could revolutionize the design of the ECO2R system and accelerate its industrial deployment.

---

## Results

To create high-energy surfaces in the catalyst, thus improving the ECO2R performance, we prepared the model catalyst SS-Ag nanoparticles (∼20−30 nm) with abundant stacking faults (SFs) and grain boundaries (GBs) (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Figs. 4–6). Aberration-corrected four-dimensional scanning TEM (STEM) (4D-STEM) revealed that abundant SFs and GBs in SS-Ag intersect with each other and result in the stepped surface formation (Fig. 2a–c and Supplementary Fig. 6). SFs and GBs finally lead to a decrease in the coordination number (CN) of Ag and an increase in lattice tensile strain (see Supplementary Figs. 7–11, Supplementary Table 8, and Supplementary Note 2). As a result, for ECO2R, SS-Ag delivered that FE towards CO reached ~99% under a wide potential window (−0.32 V to −0.65 V versus a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)) in a flow cell with the conventional electrolyte (1 M KOH) (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). We also found that the low CN and high tensile strain boosted ECO2R performance (see Supplementary Figs. 12–18 and Supplementary Note 3 for more information).

To suppress carbonate formation and crossover during ECO2R and improve the system stability, we adopted an alkali-cation-free MEA architecture with the anion- and proton-exchange membranes (AEM and PEM assembly: APMA) to evaluate the ECO2R performance of SS-Ag CP-GDE (Supplementary Fig. 19) (ref. 9). The reaction temperature was optimized at 60 °C to decrease the reaction overpotential of the pure-H2O system (Supplementary Fig. 20; the following ECO2R tests were conducted at 60 °C, unless otherwise noted).

In the alkali-cation-free APMA MEA system, at 150 mA/cm2, SS-Ag CP-GDE achieved CO and H2 FEs of ~93% and 6%, respectively (Fig. 2d, e). The cell voltage was ~3.88 V (without iR compensation for all tests in the MEA system throughout the text). In-situ Raman and isotope experiments proved that this alkali-cation-free APMA MEA system could effectively suppress carbonate formation (see Supplementary Figs. 21, 22 and Supplementary Note 4). However, the low current density (only 150 mA/cm2) resulted in a low CO2 conversion (~3.23%), drastically limiting its viability.

To increase CO2 conversion, we first decreased the CO2 inlet flow rate from 30 to 2 Standard Cubic Centimeters per Minute (sccm) (Fig. 2f). As expected, CO2 conversion gradually increased from ~3% to 43% (Fig. 2g). However, the CO FE and partial current density gradually decreased as reducing CO2 inlet flow rate (FECO: from ~93% to 82%; jCO: from ~139 to 123 mA/cm2) and those of H2 gradually increased (FEH2: from ~6% to 17%; jH2: from ~9.7 to 25.9 mA/cm2) (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. 23). That is, in this CO2 mass transport limited regime (i.e., low CO2 flow rate), the side product (H2) FE increased at the expense of that of the product (CO). The cell voltage also slightly changed from ~3.88 to 3.49 V (Fig. 2f, g). These showed that, for high CO2 conversion, a very low CO2 inlet flow rate could decrease CO2 mass transfer efficiency, leading to lower CO2/*CO coverage on the catalyst surface and thus suppressing ECO2R and increasing HER15,16. In other words, based on CP-GDE, a high CO2 inlet flow rate (i.e., fast CO2 mass transfer kinetics) could favor a higher formation rate of ECO2R product but lower the fraction of CO2 converted into product; thus, a lower CO2 conversion efficiency was observed (see Supplementary Fig. 24 and Supplementary Note 5) (refs. 17,18).

To achieve both high product selectivity and high CO2 conversion in the alkali-cation-free system, the mass transfer in the ECO2R system must be revolutionized, especially in the GDE design. Since the coverage of CO2 and the key intermediate *CO on the catalyst surface is determined by the overall flux of species both to and from the GDE surface, we re-designed and assembled an HDF-GDE by screen printing (Supplementary Fig. 25). HDF-GDE could increase the coverage of CO2 and the key intermediate *CO and overcome the mass transfer and diffusion restrictions in traditional GDEs (such as carbon paper and porous polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)) and ultimately increase the operation current density (i.e., CO2 conversion) of the alkali-cation-free system without lowering the CO2 flow rate.

To enhance the mechanical strength of HDF-GDE, a stainless-steel mesh (SSM) was used as the supporting skeleton for the catalyst sheet (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 26, 27). The porous SS-Ag HDF-GDE, whose thickness was controlled to ~300 μm by the mechanical mold, exhibited hydrophobicity due to the incorporated PTFE in the catalyst layer (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 28, 29). And HDF-GDE’s contact angle was up to ~143.9° (Supplementary Fig. 30). SS-Ag HDF-GDE only contains the catalyst, PTFE and an SSM skeleton located in the middle layer of the catalyst, allowing CO2 to directly contact the catalyst without passing through the inert substrate (such as CP and PTFE GDEs). This could essentially increase the overall flux of CO2/*CO to and from the HDF-GDE surface, accelerating the system’s mass transfer kinetics.

Upon acquiring the expected SS-Ag HDF-GDE, we evaluated its ECO2R performance in the alkali-cation-free MEA cell (Fig. 3b). The SS-Ag HDF-GDE still maintained high CO FE (~90%) at a cell voltage of ~3.19 V (Fig. 3c). More importantly, compared to SS-Ag CP-GDE, the peak current density based on SS-Ag HDF-GDE increased from 150 to 400 mA/cm2 with a negligible decline in CO FE (from ~93% to ~90%) and a slight increase in cell voltage (from ~3.88 to ~3.91 V) (Fig. 3d, f). It is worth noting that this is a pure-H2O-fed system, with a current density of 400 mA/cm2, which is even better than that of alkali-metal electrolyte systems. Additionally, HER was effectively suppressed, especially at the high current density (from ~70% to ~14% at 500 mA/cm2) (Fig. 3e). These results showed that more CO2/*CO could occupy active sites in SS-Ag while decreasing *H coverage on the catalyst surface, which improved the ECO2R activity and suppressed HER19,20. As a result, CO2 conversion efficiency on SS-Ag HDF-GDE was significantly increased to ~2.6 times without decreasing the CO2 inlet flow rate (Fig. 3g), compared with SS-Ag CP-GDE.

To verify that the improved overall flux of species to and from the HDF-GDE surface caused the increase in CO2 conversion efficiency, we investigated the CO2 mass transfer kinetics in SS-Ag HDF-GDE. On a macroscopic level, SSM possesses visible holes that are more conducive to gas transfer and diffusion than the CP-GDE substrate (Supplementary Fig. 31). On a microscopic level, although the front microporous carbon powder layer of CP-GDE can facilitate the uniform diffusion of the gas to some extent (Supplementary Fig. 32), it can also inhibit access of the gas transfer and diffusion and cause the high pressure gradient21,22, compared with SSM (Supplementary Fig. 33). Thus, when SS-Ag was assembled on different GDEs (Supplementary Fig. 34), SS-Ag CP-GDE could further limit the gas transfer and diffusion, compared to SS-Ag HDF-GDE. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images showed that SS-Ag was evenly distributed on different GDEs (Supplementary Fig. 35). The pore size of HDF-GDE was much larger than that of SS-Ag CP-GDE, which was in the micron and nano scales, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 35a–f), indicating that HDF-GDE could benefit CO2 mass transfer and diffusion, compared to that of CP-GDE.

To further verify that the fast CO2 mass transfer kinetics in HDF-GDE resulted in higher operation current density (i.e., higher CO2 conversion), rather than the higher catalyst loading, we prepared SS-Ag CP-GDE with the same catalyst loading as SS-Ag HDF-GDE (~10 mg/cm2). SS-Ag CP-GDE showed a significant decline in CO selectivity at 400 mA/cm2 with a CO FE of ~63% (Supplementary Fig. 36), compared with SS-Ag HDF-GDE (~90% CO FE). For SS-Ag CP-GDE, a high catalyst loading could inhibit CO2 access to the catalyst surface and thus suppress ECOR (i.e., low space utilization). We also investigated the effect of SS-Ag loading in HDF-GDE on ECOR performance (Supplementary Fig. 37). Catalyst loadings that are too low or too high can also significantly suppress ECOR. A low catalyst loading cannot provide enough active sites; too high a catalyst loading can also inhibit CO2 access to the catalyst surface due to the dense catalyst layer (Supplementary Fig. 38) (refs. 10,22). In addition, we employed the flow cell with 1 M KOH as the electrolyte to evaluate SS-Ag HDF-GDE ECOR performance (Supplementary Fig. 39). FE towards CO remained ~99% over a wide potential window. Still, the peak total current density increased from ~360 mA/cm2 to ~1700 mA/cm2 (Supplementary Fig. 40), compared to SS-Ag CP-GDE. These emphasized that HDF-GDE accelerated CO2 mass transfer kinetics, and that the fast CO2 mass transfer was a primary factor determining ECOR performance for SS-Ag HDF-GDE.

Further, we carried out in-situ Raman experiments to study ECO2R product (CO/*CO) coverage on different GDEs (Fig. 3h). Due to the effective CO2 mass transfer and diffusion, CO2 coverage on the HDF-GDE surface should be higher than that on the CP-GDE surface, which can cause a higher CO/*CO coverage during ECO2R9,23,24. For SS-Ag HDF-GDE, the intensity of CO/*CO located at ~230-360 cm-1 is significantly higher than that based on the SS-Ag CP-GDE, directly proving the overall flux of species both to and from HDF-GDE was increased (i.e., fast mass transfer kinetics)23,24. The high-efficiency CO2 mass transfer and diffusion can also suppress the accumulation of *H by transferring H2O on the catalyst surface, thereby improving the peak current density of ECO2R and increasing CO2 conversion without decreasing the CO2 inlet flow rate.

To quantitatively analyze mass transfer kinetics in GDEs, we simulated CO2 mass transfer. Although the models have limitations, the trend of mass transfer under the same conditions can reflect the mass transfer efficiency of different GDEs. The traditional CP-GDE contains carbon fiber and carbon powder layers with a total thickness of ~200-500 μm (Supplementary Fig. 41a) (ref. 4). Generally, the catalyst loading on CP-GDE is ~1 mg/cm2 and its thickness is ~2 μm (Supplementary Fig. 41b, c) (ref. 23). Under the real reaction environment, CO2 and products can present a concentration gradient distribution in the catalyst layer (Fig. 1a). Taking the vertical and parallel directions (dVertical and dParallel) of the catalyst layer as examples (Supplementary Fig. 41de), the closer to the cell outlet, the lower the concentration of CO2, and the opposite for products.

Under unreacted steady-state conditions, modeling of CO2 mass transfer kinetics in different GDEs showed that HDF-GDE could slightly accelerate CO2 mass transfer kinetics in the catalyst layer, compared with that of CP-GDE in both the vertical and parallel directions (Supplementary Fig. 42, see multiphysics simulation section in Supplementary information for more information). The effects of the thickness and porosity of HDF-GDE and CO2 flow rate on CO2 mass transfer were also investigated, showing that HDF-GDE’s thickness and CO2 flow rate were the two main factors influencing CO2 mass transfer efficiency under unreacted steady-state conditions (Supplementary Figs. 43–48). The GDE’s thickness was negatively correlated with CO2 mass transfer, and the CO2 inlet flow rate was positively correlated with CO2 mass transfer. Furthermore, in the vertical direction to the catalyst layer, there was almost no significant difference in CO2 mass transfer in HDF-GDE and CP-GDE (Supplementary Figs. 49–51).

When the current density of ECO2R was 150 mA/cm2, the CO2 mass transfer kinetics in GDEs were also simulated (to simplify the model, HER was not considered). At the same CO2 inlet flow rate, at the inlet, the efficiency of CO2 mass transfer to the catalyst surface in HDF-GDE was significantly higher than that in the CP-GDE in the dVertical and dParallel directions (Fig. 4a, b and Supplementary Fig. 52), indicating that CO2 coverage on the catalyst surface in HDF-GDE was higher than that in the CP-GDE at the inlet. As the reaction progressed, the CO2 coverage decreased gradually for both GDEs along the flow channel direction (Fig. 4c–e). Near the outlet, the CO2 coverage on the catalyst surface in HDF-GDE is less than in the CP-GDE. This is because, in the catalyst layer, the product (CO/*CO) coverage in HDF-GDE was higher than in the CP-GDE, which was almost a factor of magnitude difference (Fig. 4f–h and Supplementary Fig. 53). One CO2 molecule can generate one CO molecule, thus, the overall system’s mass transfer needed to consider CO2 and CO (i.e., the overall carbon concentration). Obviously, the system’s mass transfer efficiency of HDF-GDE is much higher than that of CP-GDE. Furthermore, the high carbon coverage on the catalyst surface in HDF-GDE could occupy more reaction sites, thereby decreasing the *H coverage, suppressing HER, and enhancing ECO2R-to-CO activity. In addition, the polarization curves of SS-Ag CP-GDE and HDF-GDE under N2 showed that SS-Ag HDF could indeed be capable of suppressing HER (Supplementary Fig. 54). These synergistically improved the peak operation current density for ECO2R and, thus, increased CO2 conversion.

After demonstrating ECO2R-to-CO in the alkali-cation-free MEA single cell with an SS-Ag HDF-GDE area of 1×1 cm2, we designed and customized a stack containing six MEA cells (each MEA cell with an area of 15×10 cm2) to validate the practical application possibilities of HDF-GDE combined with the alkali-cation-free MEA system (Figs. 5a–c). The scale-up demonstration and stability testing can demonstrate its practical viability, further advancing the ECO2R technology toward industrial deployment.

During scaling up, various engineering problems may arise. For example, under high power, the temperature at the MEA core can increase significantly due to resistive heating (Supplementary Table 9), and a uniform voltage distribution throughout the stack is also necessary25–28. As the power of the alkali-cation-free MEA cell stack assembled with SS-Ag HDF-GDE was scaled up to a kilowatt level, the initial temperature of pure H2O anolyte was lowered to 30 °C to balance the temperature at the MEA core and the CO2 inlet flow rate was increased to 3000 sccm.

To examine the stack’s durability, the scaled-up alkali-cation-free MEA cell stack assembled with SS-Ag HDF-GDEs was operated for 1000 h at a total current of 60 A (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. 55). The full-cell-stack voltage remained remarkably stable at 21-22 V, with an operating power of ~1.29 kW. Six SS-Ag HDF-GDEs gave a relatively stable CO FE of ~89-80% and yielded ~144 kg CO throughout the stability test (Fig. 5d). The slight voltage increase and CO FE decrease could be attributed to the mild GDE flooding under the high power. We also monitored each cell’s operation voltage, which fluctuated slightly but showed nearly the same overall voltage throughout the 1000 h measurement (Supplementary Fig. 56). The CO2 conversion in this kW-scale cell stack was up to ~81% at a CO2 inlet flow rate of 3000 sccm, which was ~25 times more than that of SS-Ag CP-GDE (~3.2%) in this single alkali-cation-free MEA cell (Fig. 3g, f, and Supplementary Table 7). Furthermore, the peak current density of HDF-GDE in the alkali-cation-free system is comparable to or even better than that of CP-GDE operated in alkali metal electrolytes (Supplementary Table 7). The stack system with HDF-GDEs achieved high CO2 conversions from ECO2R to CO at the high CO2 flow rate (Fig. 5f). We also investigated SS-Ag stability with SFs and GBs. HAADF-STEM images showed that the SS-Ag retained its structural integrity after 1000 h of ECO2R (Supplementary Fig. 57). After 1000 h of ECO2R, CP-GDE’s contact angle significantly dropped from ~137.5° to ~90.1°, while that of HDF-GDE only slightly decreased from ~143.9° to ~134.1° (Supplementary Fig. 30). The durable hydrophobicity of HDF-GDE might be due to the direct addition of PTFE to the catalyst layer, rather than just on the substrate, compared to that of CP-GDE. The stable SS-Ag catalyst, durable HDF-GDE, and alkali-cation-free MEA system, along with fast mass transfer kinetics in HDF-GDE, synergistically boosted ECO2R performance.

We sought to selectively convert CO2 to C2H4 using a Cu electrocatalyst, given the high value and broad applications of C2H4 in the chemical industry. Based on our previously reported SS-Cu9, we fabricated SS-Cu HDF-GDE. We evaluated its ECO2R-to-C2H4 performance in the alkali-cation-free MEA cell (Supplementary Fig. 58). The peak C2H4 FE reached ~45% with a cell voltage of ~4.36 V, comparable to SS-Cu CP-GDE (FE: ~43%; cell voltage: ~4.30 V)9, but the total current density was increased from 300 to 500 mA/cm2 (ref. 9), indicating that the HDF-GDE strategy was also suitable for alkali-cation-free ECO2R-to-C2H4/C2+. At a total current of 75 A, the stability of the kW-scale (~1.95 kW) alkali-cation-free APMA MEA cell stack assembled with 6 SS-Cu HDF-GDEs was also over 1000 h, yielding ~14 kg C2H4 (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Figs. 59, 60). And ECO2R-to-C2H4 conversion in this alkali-cation-free APMA MEA cell stack increased to approximately ~15 times, compared to the SS-Cu CP-GDE in the initial single APMA MEA cell9. For both SS-Ag and SS-Cu (ECO2R-to-CO/C2H4), HDF-GDEs improved CO2 conversion efficiency by increasing ECO2R current density rather than decreasing the CO2 inlet flow rate, while maintaining high product selectivity, effectively alleviating the trade-off between high product selectivity and high CO2 conversion. Furthermore, the operating current density of the pure-H2O-fed (alkali-cation-free) system was effectively exceeded.

The rapid acceleration toward commercially viable ECO2R-to-CO/C2H4 necessitates techno-economic analysis (TEA) to identify key areas for improvement. Thus, an industrial-level TEA based on the performance of our durable alkali-cation-free kW-scale ECO2R-to-CO/C2H4 system was provided (see the Techno-economic analysis section in Supplementary information for more information). TEA includes additional costs for gaseous product purification, assuming unreacted CO2 is separated and recycled as fresh feedstock. The kW-scale alkali-cation-free ECO2R-to-CO is economically viable with a levelized CO cost of ~0.48 USD/kg (Supplementary Fig. 61a), which is below the market price of ~0.6 USD/kg (ref. 3). Our alkali-cation-free kW-scale ECO2R-to-CO system is competitive with the systems with CsHCO3 as the electrolyte3. The most significant advantage of the alkali-cation-free system is its high stability. With a longer lifetime (5-year MEA replacement period) for the alkali-cation-free APMA system assembled with HDF-GDEs, the levelized CO cost can be reduced by an additional 13% (~0.42 USD/kg). The MEA lifetime is negatively correlated with product cost (Supplementary Fig. 62). Compared with SS-Ag CP-GDE, the HDF-GDE strategy reduced the cost of ECO2R-to-CO by 35% (Supplementary Fig. 61a). Electricity consumption is the most significant contributor to the levelized cost of CO production. Sensitivity analysis shows that a 20% increase in electricity price leads to an over 10% rise in the levelized CO cost (Supplementary Fig. 61b). Other economic parameters, such as the MEA replacement period and CO2 price, affect the final TEA result by less than 5% with a 20% fluctuation.

The choice of electricity sources can also impact the economic viability of the ECO2R-to-CO system. Electricity from coal combustion with carbon capture and storage is over 300% more expensive than the lowest-cost option, making it economically unacceptable. The significant uncertainty in renewable energy sources, such as wind power, leads to varied outcomes regarding the economic viability of the alkali-cation-free ECO2R system (see Supplementary Fig. 63).

For ECO2R-to-C2H4, although the alkali-cation-free system assembled with HDF-GDEs was competitive with the reference study, which used KHCO3 as an electrolyte28,29, the levelized C2H4 cost reached ~5.63 USD/kg, exceeding the market price of ~1.0 USD/kg (refs. 4,28), which is due to the low C2H4 selectivity in the alkali-cation-free system. With an assumed extended 5-year lifetime for the MEA, the levelized C2H4 cost can be further reduced by ~10% (Supplementary Fig. 61c). Taking into account the market value of the byproducts (H2 and CO), the C2H4 cost can be lowered to ~1.66 USD/kg. The economic roadmap proposes that implementing a carbon tax of 60 USD/ton and reducing electricity prices (based on China’s green electricity at 0.2 CNY/kWh) can render alkali-cation-free ECO2R-to-C2H4 economically viable at ~0.48 USD/kg. Together, from TEA, the alkali-cation-free ECO2R system assembled with HDF-GDEs can achieve economic viability at scale for ECO2R-to-CO/C2H4.

## Methods

Chemicals and materials
Iridium(IV) oxide (IrO2, ≥ 99.9%, 206237), NafionTM solution (5 wt.%, 274704), 3-(Trimethylsilyl)propionic-2,2,3,3-d4 acid sodium salt (TSP, ≥ 98.0% (NMR), 269913), Polytetrafluoroethylene preparation (PTFE solution, 60% in H2O, 665800), Deuterium oxide (D2O, 99.9 at.% D, 151882), Silver nitrate (AgNO3, ≥ 99.0%, 209139), Water-18O (H218O, ≥ 10 at.% 18O, 332089), α−terpineol (90%, 432628), 2-(2-butoxyethoxy)ethanol (≥ 99%, 579963), Oleylamine (70%, O7805), acetone (≥ 99.5%, 179124), Copper(I) chloride (CuCl, 97%, 212946), n-hexane (C6H14, 99%, HX0293), Octadecylamine (≥ 99%, 305391), Ethyl 2-cyanoacrylate (E1505, 7085-85-0), Trioctylphosphine (90%, 117854) and squalane (96%, 234311) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The alkaline ionomer solution (5% in ethanol, Sustainion XA-9) and anion exchange membrane (Sustainion X37-50) were purchased from Dioxide Materials. Potassium hydroxide (KOH, ≥ 85.0%), stainless-steel mesh (SSM, 0.10 mm thickness, 500×500 mesh; warp, ~25 μm) and Titanium fiber felt (0.25 mm thickness, 99.9%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. (China). Acrylic resin (E0545) was purchased from Shenzhen JITIAN Chemical Co., LTD. Isopropanol (C3H8O, IPA, ≥ 99.5%, 3776) was purchased from Fisher Scientific. The anion exchange membrane (Fumasep FAA-3-PK-75), gas diffusion layer (carbon paper, GDE, Sigracet 39BC), and Nafion® 117 membrane (591239) were purchased from Fuel Cell Store.

Catalyst synthesis
In a typical synthesis, 0.07 g of AgNO3 and 0.02 g of octadecylamine were dissolved in 0.8 mL of squalane, and the solution was heated for 0.5 h at 80 °C under an inert gas (Ar) atmosphere to form an Ag-based stock solution. Meanwhile, a mixed solution of 10 mL oleylamine and 0.04 mL trioctylphosphine was heated to 170 °C under an Ar atmosphere with vigorous magnetic agitation. Subsequently, the Ag-based stock solution was injected into the above mixture and heated to 170 °C for 5 h. After natural cooling, the resulting sample was collected by centrifugation and washed several times with n-hexane. Finally, the sample was dried at 80 °C in a vacuum before use. The sample was denoted as SS-Ag.

The SS-Ag samples were annealed at various temperatures (250, 350, and 450 °C) in the tube furnace for 2 h under a mixed gas (H2/Ar: 5 v/v%; 200 sccm), denoted as Ag-250, Ag-350, and Ag-450, respectively.

The Cu sample (SS-Cu) was also prepared by the above method, using a Cu-based stock solution (CuCl) instead of the Ag-based stock solution, and the reaction temperature was increased to 200 °C (see ref. 9 for more detailed information).

GDEs fabrication
For conventional/traditional CP-GDEs in the flow cell, carbon paper (Sigracet 39BC) served as the gas diffusion layer. The cathode catalyst was dispersed in a mixed solution of H2O and IPA (1:4 v/v) and a NafionTM solution (~3 wt.% vs. catalyst) by sonication for 1 h to form the catalyst ink (1 mg/mL). Then, the catalyst ink was sprayed onto the microporous carbon layer of the carbon paper at a catalyst loading of 1–3 mg/cm2, followed by drying at 120 °C under vacuum for 1 h before testing. The anode GDE using the commercial IrO2 as the anode catalyst was also prepared by the above method.

For conventional/traditional CP-GDEs used in the APMA MEA cell with pure H2O as the anolyte, the NafionTM solution in the cathode catalyst ink was replaced by an alkaline ionomer solution (Sustainion XA-9), and nothing else changed. In addition, Ir-supported Ti fiber felt (Ir/Ti) was used as the anode electrode. Ir was sputtered on the Ti fiber felt using a pure Ir target in an Ar environment (5×10-3 Torr) in a magnetron sputtering system. Then, Ir/Ti was pressed onto the carbon paper to form the anode GDE.

For high-diffusion-flux (HDF) GDEs, the cathode catalyst (SS-Ag/SS-Cu) was printed onto the SSM skeleton by screen printing, followed by vacuum drying overnight. After that, the SSM-skeleton-supported catalyst was pressed at 1000 pounds of pressure for 2 h and the thickness of the HDF-GDE was controlled to ~300 μm. Finally, it was calcined at 350 °C for 30 min. The printing ink was prepared by mixing the catalyst and PTFE solution with an organic solution consisting of α-terpineol, 2-(2-butoxyethoxy)ethanol, and acrylic resin, with an approximate weight ratio of 65:15:20. The catalyst loading in HDF-GDE was controlled to about 10 mg/cm2.

Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction measurements
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (ECO2R) in the flow cell was to employ an electrochemical workstation (CHI 660E) connected to a current booster (CHI 680C). The CO2 flow rate (30 sccm, unless otherwise noted) was controlled by a mass flow controller (MFC, Alicat Scientific MC). The electrolyte (1 M KOH, pH = ~14) flow rate was ~10 mL/min, controlled by a peristaltic pump. The cathode area in the flow cell was 1 cm×1 cm. The flow cell consists of two titanium gas flow channels, two PTFE buffer layers, a membrane (Fumasep FAA-3-PK-75) between the two buffer layers, two titanium current collectors, and two aluminum end plates. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel to guide the CO2 stream and conduct the electricity. The serpentine flow channel is featured with a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. Both cathode and anode chambers have two 0.5-cm-thick PTFE buffer layers, through which the 1 M KOH electrolyte stream flows. All ECO2R measurements in the flow cell were carried out at room temperature and the Hg/Hg2Cl2 (SCE, saturated KCl) was used as the reference electrode, and all cathode potentials (vs. Hg/Hg2Cl2) were converted to the RHE scale via the following Eq. 1:

E(RHE) = E(Hg/Hg2Cl2) + 0.241 + 0.0591 × pH + iR (1)

where R is the resistance between the cathode and reference electrodes in the flow cell measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) with a frequency range from 105 Hz to 0.01 Hz at the working potential.

For ECO2R in the single MEA cell, pure H2O (pH = ~7) was used as the anolyte. The cathode area in the flow cell was 1 cm×1 cm. The MEA cell consists of two titanium gas flow channels and a membrane between the cathode and the anode. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel, which has a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. The cathode and anode GDEs were separated by an AEM (Sustainion X37-50) and a PEM (Nafion 117) assembly (APMA architecture). The areas of both AEM and PEM are 2 cm×2 cm. AEM with a dry thickness of ~50 μm is soaked in 1 M KOH solution for storage and is washed with water before use. For the PEM with a dry thickness of ~183 μm, it was soaked in ~3% hydrogen peroxide for 1 h at 80 °C, deionized water for 1 h at 80 °C, and 0.5 M H2SO4 for another 1 h at 80 °C. And the resulting PEM was cleaned and preserved in deionized water at room temperature. Therein, the cathode GDE and the anode GDE were in contact with the AEM and the PEM, respectively. Cell voltages were directly presented without iR compensation for all MEA measurements. The reaction temperature was set at 60 °C. Unless otherwise noted, other reaction conditions were the same as those tested in the flow cell.

For scaled-up APMA-MEA stack measurements, an integrated circuit based on the Arduino UNO R3 (A000066) was used as an aid for monitoring, connected to the CoolTerm serial terminal application. The scaled-up APMA-MEA stack consists of two titanium gas flow channels and membranes between the cathode and the anode. The titanium gas flow channel is engraved with a serpentine flow channel, which has a width of 1 mm and an interval of 1 mm. All ECO2R measurements in the APMA-MEA stack were performed using the customized Variable DC power supply (10 kW). The cathode area was 150 cm2. The flow rates of the anolyte and CO2 were 20 mL/min and 3000 sccm, respectively. The initial temperature of the pure H2O anolyte was set to 30 °C rather than 60 °C due to the higher heat generation from the stack at high power. AEM (Sustainion X37-50) was replaced by one (MTCP-50) for the high stability30. Full-cell-stack voltages were directly presented without iR compensation. Unless otherwise noted, other reaction conditions were the same as those tested in the single MEA cell.

Products analysis
For ECO2R, the gas and liquid products were quantified by gas chromatography (GC, GC-2030, Shimadzu) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, ECZ500R, 500 MHz, JEOL), respectively. GC was equipped with two thermal conductivity detectors (TCDs) for H2, O2, N2, He, CO, and CO2 signals, and a flame ionization detector (FID) for CH4, C2H4, and C2H6 signals. GC was composed of packed columns of two Porapak-N, a Molecular sieve-13X, a Molecular sieve-5A, a Porapak-Q and an HP-PLOT AL/S, and employed He (99.999%) and N2 (99.999%) as the carrier gases. Ar was used as the internal standard to calibrate the CO2 flow rate at the cell outlet (fCO2), which was fed at 2 sccm and mixed with the cell outlet gas stream before injection into GC23. The FEs of gas products were calculated by the following Eq. 2:

FE(%) = N_x × F × m_x × f_CO2 / j_Total × 100% (2)

where N_x is the number of electrons transferred for the specific product (x), F is the Faradaic constant, m_x is the molar fraction of the specific product (x) determined by GC, f_CO2 is the molar flow rate of the CO2, and j_Total is the total current density.

The liquid products were analyzed by 500 MHz 1H NMR spectroscopy (ECZ500R, JEOL) with water suppression. TSP and D2O were used as the reference standard and lock solvent, respectively. The FEs of liquid products were calculated by the following Eq. 3:

FE(%) = N_x × F × C_x × V_x / Q_Total × 100% (3)

where N_x is the number of electrons transferred for the specific liquid product (x), F is the Faradaic constant, C_x is the concentration of the specific liquid product (x) determined by 1H NMR, V_x is the volume of the electrolyte, and Q_Total is the total charge.

CO2 conversion was calculated using the following Eqs. 4–6:

f_x = F_x / (N_total × t × x_A) (4)

For SS-Ag catalyst:

CO2 Conversion (%) = f_CO2 / f_CO2_inlet × 100% (5)

For SS-Cu catalyst:

CO2-to-C2H4 Conversion (%) = 2 × f_C2H4 / f_CO2_inlet × 100% (6)

where f_x is the molar rate of the product (x) formation, t is the electrolysis reaction time, and A is the geometric area of the electrode.

Multiphysics simulation
The simulation was performed using COMSOL Multiphysics v. 5.6. The ECO2R process at the cathode was simulated under a fixed inlet flow rate, steady-state conditions, and involves two half-reactions: ECO2R-to-CO and HER (Eqs. 7 and 8). Although HER can affect CO2 diffusion through convection between H2 and CO2, the resulting diffusion trends for CO2 and H2 are in agreement. Thus, to simplify the calculation, Eq. 8 was not considered during the simulation.

CO2 + H2O + 2e− → CO + 2OH− (7)

2H2O + 2e− → H2 + 2OH− (8)

The momentum conservation in the serpentine channel, porous gas diffusion electrode and catalyst layer is expressed by the compressible Navier-Stokes equation31 and Darcy’s law32, respectively (Eqs. 9–11):

ρ∇·u = 0 (9)

ρ(u·∇)u = ∇·[−pI + μ(∇u + (∇u)T)] (10)

μ/K u + ∇p = 0 (11)

where ρ, u, p and μ represent density, flow velocity, gauge pressure and dynamic viscosity, respectively. K represents the permeability of the porous structure, including the GDE and catalyst layer, which can be expressed as (Eq. 12):

K = d_f^2 × ε^3 / K_CK(1−ε)^2 (12)

where ε is the porosity, d_f is the mean fiber diameter or the size of the particle, and K_CK is the Carman-Kozeny constant. The specific surface area (a) (ref. 33) of the porous structure can be expressed as (Eq. 13):

a = 4(1−ε) / d_f (13)

The mass transfer of gas in the porous structure and the flow channel involves both convection and diffusion. Therefore, the mass transfer process of all participating particles can be expressed by the Maxwell-Stefan equation (Eqs. 14–18) (ref. 34):

∇·j_i + ρ(u·∇)ω_i = R_i (14)

j_i = −(ρω_i Σ D_ik ∇x_k + D_i^T ∇T / T) (15)

d_k = ∇x_k + [(x_k − ω_k) ∇p / p] (16)

x_k = ω_k / M_k / Σ (ω_i / M_i) (17)

ω_i = c_i M_i / ρ (18)

where the subscript i represents species type. j_i is the relative mass flux vector, ω_i is the mass fraction, D_ik is the Maxwell-Stefan diffusion coefficient, d_k is the diffusional driving force, D_i^T is the thermal diffusion coefficient, x_k is the molar fraction, M_i is the reciprocal of the molar mass, and p is the absolute pressure.

The transport of current in the electrocatalysis process occurs via electron transport at the electrodes. Therefore, they can be calculated through Ohm’s law (Eq. 19):

i_s = −σ_eff^s ∇φ_s (19)

where i_s and φ_s are the current density and potential, respectively. And the relationship between effective conductivity (σ_eff^s) and electrode material conductivity (σ_s) can be expressed by the Bruggeman correlation (Eq. 20) (ref. 35):

σ_eff^s = (1−ε)^1.5 σ_s (20)

The relationship of electrochemical reaction kinetics in the catalyst layer is described by the Butler-Volmer equation (Eq. 21) (ref. 36):

i_cs = i_0 [ (c_CO2 / c_CO2_ref) exp(α_c F η_c / RT) − (c_CO / c_CO_ref) exp(α_a F η_c / RT) ] (21)

where the i_cs stands for the transfer current density of the cathode. c_i and c_i_ref are the surface concentration and bulk concentration of the porous structure, respectively. α_c and η_c are the cathode charge transfer coefficient and the cathode overpotential, respectively. Here, i_0 represents the exchange current density of the cathode, which can be given as follows (Eq. 22) (ref. 36):

i_0 = F · k_c · (c_CO2)^α_c · (c_CO)^α_a (22)

where the k_c is the electrochemical reaction rate constant.

The overpotential can be expressed as follows (Eq. 23):

η_c = φ_s − φ_l − E_eq (23)

where subscripts s and l represent the solid phase and liquid phase, respectively. E_eq stands for the equilibrium potential. The Nernst equation can be used to describe the equilibrium potential as follows (Eq. 24):

E_eq = E^0 + RT / nF ln(c_CO2 / c_CO) (24)

where E^0 represents the standard electrode potential of the cathode versus the standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K.

Boundary conditions for the cathode half-reaction in the alkali-cation-free APMA system are as follows. The galvanostatic condition was used during the electrocatalytic process; hence, a constant current density was utilized on the current collector. In addition, a fixed mass flux (Q) and species mass fraction of CO2 were set at the inlet boundary and other boundary conditions were listed in Supplementary Table 1. The relevant transport parameters in the present simulation are listed in Supplementary Table 2. To ensure the numerical model accurately simulates the electrochemical reaction process, the electrochemical reaction validation was carried out under fixed operating conditions.

It can be seen that, across different CO2 inlet flow rates, the simulated CO/CO2 outlet flow rate is in good agreement with the experimental data (Supplementary Fig. 1). The slight deviation maybe attributed to the model’s omission of a side reaction. Therefore, the model could be used to simulate the electrochemical reaction process. Techno-economic analysis
The TEA of the CO2 electrolysis system is based on published models37,38, with slight adjustments to account for the recycling of unreacted CO2, thereby offsetting the cost of purchasing CO2. An industrial-scale production capacity of 50,000 kg/day is assumed. The actual single-pass conversion rate of CO2, derived from experimental studies, was utilized in the calculations. A pressure swing adsorption (PSA) unit was virtually designed to purify gaseous products from both the cathode and anode. The capital investment for the PSA unit was estimated based on reference costs, and its operating expenditure was calculated at 0.23 kWh per m3/h of gas mixture39. For typical electrodes, the membrane replacement cost was simplified to be 1180 $/m2 for all cases39. The parameters and assumptions used for TEA are summarized in Supplementary Table 4 and the TEA results are listed in Supplementary Tables 5 and 6.

The levelized cost of carbon monoxide production (LCOC) is employed as the techno-economic indicator, as defined in Eq. 25.

LCOC = Σ (TAC + OPEX_r)t / Σ (PD + D_r)t (25)

where TAC and WCP are the total annual cost and working capital, respectively. BAL is the balance of the plant. PD is the annual amount of product generated, which is 5000 kg/day for all case studies. r is the nominal interest rate and n is the plant lifetime.

Total annual cost is composed of the operating expenditure OPEX, and the depreciation cost DEP of the capital assets, as defined in Eq. 26.

TAC = OPEX + DEP (26)

where the calculation of OPEX includes the purchase cost of electricity and water, the replacement cost of membrane and stack, the purchase cost of carbon dioxide, maintenance cost, and operating expenses of the PSA unit. The depreciation rate of capital assets is assumed to average 10% annually until reaching 20% of the end-of-life salvage value of the facility37.
